intro: IELTS Reading matnni ko'chirib yozishni emas, MA'NONI tanishni tekshiradi. Shuning uchun savolda bir so'z, matnda esa uning sinonimi turadi. Bu — paraphrase.
Misol: savolda "people who live there", matnda "residents". Ma'no bir xil, so'z boshqa.
Qoida: SAVOLNI o'zgartirmang, MATNNI qidiring. Avval savoldan kalit so'zni belgilang (ot, fe'l, raqam, ism), keyin matndan o'sha ma'noni qidiring.
Javobni yozganda esa aksincha: javob MATNDAGI so'z bilan yoziladi. O'zingizning sinonimingiz — noto'g'ri javob.
4 xil paraphrase: 1) sinonim (money — cash); 2) so'z turkumi o'zgaradi (costs less — is cheaper); 3) antonim + inkor (shallow — not deep); 4) umumiy so'z (Candela, Ponga — small villages).
Ism, raqam, sana va joy nomlari paraphrase qilinmaydi — ular matnda xuddi o'sha holda turadi. Shuning uchun ular eng tez topiladigan "langar" (anchor) hisoblanadi.

readings.title: The World's Friendliest City
text: A team of social psychologists from California has spent six years studying the reactions of people in cities around the world to different situations. The results show that cities where people _have less_ money generally have friendlier _populations_. Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, which is often _known for_ its crime, comes out top, and the capital of Malawi, Lilongwe, comes third.
But what makes one city friendlier than another? The psychologists from California State University say it has got more to do with environment than culture or nationality.

They carried out a study into the way locals treated strangers in 23 cities around the world. The team conducted their research through a series of tests, where they dropped pens or pretended they were blind and needed help crossing the street.

The study concludes that people are more helpful in cities with a more relaxed _way of life_ such as Rio. While they were there, researchers received help in 93 percent of cases, and the percentage in Lilongwe was only a little lower. However, richer cities such as Amsterdam and New York are considered the least friendly. Inhabitants of Amsterdam helped the researchers in 53 percent of cases and in New York just 44 percent. The psychologists found that, in these cities, people tend to _be short of_ time, so they hurry and often _ignore_ strangers.

readings.title: The Best Cities in the World
text: In a recent internet survey, tourists and business travellers were asked to rate 50 cities around the world, from the best to the worst. Of the top three cities, two were in Europe and one was in Australia.

In third place was London, scoring highly mainly because it was the most _famous_ city on the list of 50 surveyed. It was also seen as a very _good place_ to do business, and was an important cultural centre. However, it lost points because people believed it was an _extremely_ expensive place to live.

Sydney was also a very popular destination, achieving second place on the list because people believed it had the friendliest _inhabitants_, as well as the best _standard of living_ and the _nicest_ climate. It failed to make the top spot, however, because people thought there were _very few_ things to see there, and many also thought it was too far away from other business and cultural centres.

At the top of the list was Paris. Despite problems such as the _large amount of_ traffic, it beat other cities to first place because people considered it to be the most interesting city, with more museums, art galleries and places of interest than anywhere else. People also thought it was the best city to take a holiday in.

readings.title: The city that pays you to live there
text: In 2019, the small town of Candela in southern Italy had a problem. Young people were leaving for the big cities, and only about 2,700 residents remained. Shops closed, the school lost half its pupils, and the streets were quiet even in summer. So the mayor tried something unusual: he offered money to anyone who moved there. A single person received 800 euros, a couple 1,200 euros, and a family with children up to 2,000 euros. The only conditions were that newcomers had to rent or buy a house in the town and find work that paid at least 7,500 euros a year.

The idea worked better than anyone expected. Within a year, more than fifty families had applied, and the town hall received phone calls from as far away as Brazil. Candela is not rich, but it is safe, the air is clean, and a two-bedroom flat costs less than a parking space in Milan. For families with small children, that difference matters more than a high salary.

Other places have copied the plan. In Japan, the government of a mountain village gives free land to anyone who builds a house and stays for ten years. In Spain, the village of Ponga pays 3,000 euros to each couple who moves in, plus 3,000 more for every baby born there. Officials in these places say the aim is not tourism but population: a village without children has no future.

Not everyone is convinced. Critics point out that money brings people for a year or two, but only jobs keep them. In Candela, about a third of the new arrivals left again when their contracts ended. The mayor agrees, but he says the town is still better off than before: the school has reopened its second class, and two cafés now stay open until midnight.

readings.title: Where the streets have no cars
text: Pontevedra is a medium-sized city in the north-west of Spain. Thirty years ago its narrow streets were full of traffic: about 14,000 cars passed through the old centre every day, the air was dirty, and between 1990 and 1996 thirty people died in road accidents. In 1999 a new mayor, who had worked as a doctor, decided that the centre belonged to people rather than to vehicles. Cars were not banned, but parking in the middle of the city was removed, speed limits were cut to 30 kilometres an hour, and pavements were widened.

The results surprised the rest of Europe. Traffic in the centre fell by around 90 per cent, and carbon dioxide emissions dropped by two thirds. Since 2011 nobody has been killed in a traffic accident inside the city. Shops, which had been afraid of losing customers, now report more visitors, because people who walk stop more often than people who drive.

The city also changed the way children travel to school. A scheme called "Metrominuto" gives every family a map that looks like an underground railway map, but the coloured lines show walking routes and the time each journey takes: eight minutes from the market to the town hall, twelve minutes from the station to the park. Today about seven out of ten children walk to school without an adult, a figure almost unknown in other European cities.

Pontevedra is not perfect. Some older residents complain that deliveries are slower, and drivers from nearby villages say they must park far from the shops. Yet the population of the centre has grown by 12,000 since the changes began, while many other Spanish old towns have emptied.

readings.title: The quietest city in the world
text: Noise is not only unpleasant; it is dangerous. The World Health Organization says that long periods of loud sound raise blood pressure, damage sleep and, in European cities, shorten thousands of lives every year. Anything above 65 decibels during the day is considered harmful. A busy road reaches about 80 decibels, and a motorcycle passing close by reaches 95.

For this reason a number of cities now measure noise as carefully as they measure air pollution. Zurich, in Switzerland, is usually named the quietest large city in Europe. Its trams run on rubber-covered rails, rubbish is collected before seven in the morning only in the outer districts, and building work must stop at eight in the evening. Residents can report noise through a mobile application, and the city answers within 48 hours.

The opposite example is often said to be Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh, where the average street noise reaches 119 decibels — louder than a rock concert. Most of it comes from car horns. Drivers use the horn as a greeting, a warning and a complaint, sometimes more than a thousand times an hour on a single street. In 2020 the government tried a "no horn" day; the noise fell by only 5 per cent, because most drivers ignored it.

Solutions do exist, and they are cheaper than people expect. Trees along a road cut noise by up to 10 decibels. Rubber road surfaces cut it by 5. In South Korea, some flats now have "quiet floors" made of thick material, after complaints between neighbours became one of the most common reasons for arguments in the whole country.

readings.title: Reading #3. The happiest country in the world
text: Children growing up in Costa Rica are surrounded by some of the most beautiful and diverse landscapes in the world. Preserving tropical rainforests isn't Costa Rica's only success, because the government also makes sure everyone has access to health-care and education. So when the New Economics Foundation released its second Happy Planet Index, Costa Rica came out number one. The index is a ranking of countries based on their _impact_ on the environment and the health and happiness of their _citizens_.

According to Mariano Rojas, a Costa Rican economics professor, Costa Rica is a mid-income country where citizens have plenty of time for themselves and for their relationships with others. 'A mid-income level allows most citizens to satisfy their basic needs. The government makes sure that all Costa Ricans have access to education, health and nutrition services.' Costa Ricans, he believes, are not interested in status or spending money to show how successful they are.

_Created_ in 2008, the Happy Planet Index examines happiness on a national level and _ranks_ 143 countries according to three measurements: their citizens' happiness, how long they live (which reflects their health), and _how much_ of the planet's resources each country _consumes_. According to researcher Saamah Abdallah, the Index also measures the outcomes that are most important, and those are happy, healthy lives for everyone.
paraphrases: how long they live (reflects their health)

readings.title: Reading #4. A city survey with a difference
text: There are many websites on the Internet which provide lists of the world's best cities to visit, live or work in. These lists usually grade the cities in order, from 'best' to 'worst', and are based on facts and figures provided by local or national organisations.

The City Brands Index (CBI) also provides a list of best and worst cities. However, unlike other surveys, it is based on the idea that cities are _similar to_ products in shops. It asks ordinary people in other countries to grade cities in the same way that they would grade a product, like a soft drink or a car. What is particularly different about the CBI is that the people who take part in the survey may not have ever visited the cities. Instead, they are asked to say what they think the cities are like, basing their opinions on things like news stories, magazine articles or television programmes they have heard or seen.

_Each_ year, about 10,000 people in 20 countries take part in the CBI survey, and they grade a _total_ of 50 cities. They do this by filling in an online questionnaire. There are _several_ categories in the survey. These include things like the economy, education, the environment, local culture, climate and what the city's residents are like.

The CBI list is _useful_ because it helps people choose a good place to live, _find work_ or take a holiday. It also helps _regional_ governments to understand why people and businesses are, or are not, coming to their cities, and so shows them areas which they could develop or improve.

readings.title: The country that measures happiness instead of money
text: Most governments judge success by one number: how much the economy grows each year. Bhutan, a small kingdom in the Himalayas with about 780,000 people, does something different. Since 1972 it has used a measure called Gross National Happiness, and in 2008 this idea was written into the country's new constitution.

The measure has four main parts: fair economic development, protection of the environment, care for culture, and good government. Every few years officials visit homes across the country and ask each family a long list of questions. The survey takes around three hours per household and covers thirty-three indicators, from sleep and health to trust in neighbours.

The environmental rule is the strictest in the world. The constitution says that at least 60 per cent of the land must stay under forest for ever; today the real figure is about 71 per cent. Because the forests absorb more carbon than the country produces, Bhutan is one of the few carbon-negative nations on Earth.

The system has problems too. Young people leave for Australia and India, where salaries are five or six times higher, and unemployment among graduates reached 29 per cent in 2022. Critics say happiness is difficult to measure and easy to use in advertising. Officials answer that no number is perfect, but a country that counts only money will protect only money.

readings.title: The library that lends everything except books
text: In the Canadian city of Toronto there is a library where the shelves hold no novels. Instead, members borrow tools: drills, ladders, sewing machines, tents and even musical instruments. The Toronto Tool Library opened in 2013 with 150 tools donated by local families. Today it holds more than 10,000 items and has about 5,000 members, who pay a yearly fee of 50 dollars.

The idea is simple. An electric drill is used, on average, for only thirteen minutes in its entire life, yet almost every household owns one. Sharing a single drill among fifty families saves money and space, and it also cuts waste: fewer machines are built, and fewer are thrown away.

Similar libraries have opened in more than 500 cities worldwide. In Berlin, one branch lends camping equipment; in Melbourne, another lends party supplies such as tables and lights. The most popular item almost everywhere is the pressure washer, which is expensive to buy and needed perhaps twice a year.

Running such a library is harder than it looks. Tools break, and repairs take up a quarter of the budget. Some members keep items too long, so most branches now charge a small fine for every day an item is late. Staff also teach short courses — how to fix a bicycle, how to use a saw safely — and these classes bring in nearly half of the income at the Toronto branch.

readings.title: Living on a floating island
text: Lake Titicaca lies between Peru and Bolivia, 3,812 metres above sea level. On the Peruvian side live the Uros people, whose homes stand on about 120 artificial islands made entirely of totora, a reed that grows in the shallow water near the shore.

Building an island takes a community around one year. First, blocks of root and soil are cut from the lake bed and tied together with rope; these blocks float because they contain gas. Reeds are then laid on top in layers, each layer crossing the one below. A finished island is roughly two metres thick, but the surface reed rots quickly, so fresh reeds must be added every two weeks in the rainy season.

Life on the islands has changed. Fifty years ago most families lived by fishing and hunting birds. Today around 2,000 people live on the islands and most income comes from tourism: nearly 200,000 visitors arrive each year, and many islands now have solar panels, which power lights and a television. The largest island has a school, a small hospital and a radio station.

There are worries. Young Uros often move to the city of Puno for work or study, and the reed beds are shrinking because of warmer water and pollution. A local guide explains the problem simply: the islands survive only while somebody keeps adding reeds.

readings.title: Reading #5. Freya Stark, explorer and writer
text: Freya Stark travelled to many areas of the Middle East, often alone.

Freya Stark was an explorer who lived during a time when explorers were regarded as heroes. She travelled to distant areas of the Middle East, where few Europeans - especially women - had travelled before. She also travelled extensively in Turkey, Greece, Italy, Nepal and Afghanistan.

Stark was born in Paris in 1893. Although she had no formal education as a child, she moved about with her artist parents and learned French, German and Italian. She entered London University in 1912, but at the start of World War I, she joined the nurse corps and was sent to Italy. After the war, she returned to London and attended the School of Oriental Studies. Her studies there led to extensive travel in the Middle East, enabling her to eventually become fluent in Persian, Russian and Turkish.
Stark became well known as a traveler and explorer in the Middle East. She travelled to the Lebanon in 1927 at the age of 33 when she had saved enough money, and while there, she studied Arabic.

In 1928, she travelled by donkey to the Jebel Druze, a mountainous area in Syria. During another trip, she went to a distant region of the Elburz, a mountain range in Iran, where she made a map. She was searching for information about an ancient Muslim sect known as the Assassins, which she wrote about in Valley of the Assassins (1934), a classic for which she was awarded a Gold Medal by the Royal Geographic Society. For the next 12 years, she continued her career as a traveler and writer, establishing a style which combined an account of her journeys with personal commentary on the people, places, customs, history and politics of the Middle East.

readings.title: Reading #7. Patrick Malone (Part 1)
text: Patrick Malone is a traveller, writer and broadcaster. He was born in 1968 in Basel, Switzerland, where his British parents were working for a pharmaceutical company. His family left Switzerland when he was twelve, and returned to their home in Britain. For the next six years, Malone attended the local secondary school. He then went to Leeds University to do a course in Human Geography. He wanted to become a town planner. However, the only work he could find was as a teacher at a local school.

During his holidays and free time, he went walking, often covering very long distances very quickly. On one occasion he walked the entire length of Britain, a distance of over 1,400 kilometres, in less than a month. He enjoyed the experience and the challenge so much that he started walking in different parts of the world, usually in fairly remote areas away from major population centres. The people he met and the experiences he had on these trips provided him with some excellent material for his classes.

It was during one trip that he met his old university tutor, Don Perkins. At the time, Perkins was putting together a team of geographers and biologists for a research trip to the Amazon, and asked Malone if he would like to go with them. The expedition was for a whole year, and so he had to give up his job at the school, but Malone did not hesitate to accept Perkins' offer. He sold his car to make some money, bought an airline ticket for Brazil and set off.

readings.title: How a pencil is made
text: The ordinary pencil looks simple, but making one takes about a week and passes through nine machines. The process begins in a forest in California, where cedar trees are cut after roughly sixty years of growth. Cedar is chosen because it is soft enough to sharpen but strong enough not to break.

First, the wood is cut into flat boards called slats, each about 18 centimetres long. The slats are then dried for several days and covered with wax, which makes cutting easier later. Next, a machine cuts eight narrow grooves along each slat.

While this is happening, the "lead" is prepared in a different part of the factory. Despite its name, it contains no lead at all: it is a mixture of graphite and clay. The two powders are mixed with water, pressed into long thin strings and baked in an oven at about 800 degrees. More clay makes a harder, lighter line; more graphite makes a softer, darker one.

After baking, the strings are laid in the grooves of one slat, and a second slat is glued on top, so that the lead is trapped between two pieces of wood. Once the glue is dry, a cutting machine separates the sandwich into individual pencils, which are still square. The pencils are then shaped, painted with up to eight layers of paint, and finally stamped with the brand name. A rubber is added last, held in place by a small metal ring.

readings.title: From bean to bar: making chocolate
text: Chocolate starts as a seed inside a large fruit called a pod, which grows directly on the trunk of the cacao tree. A healthy tree produces about thirty pods a year, and each pod holds roughly forty seeds, usually called beans. Because the pods do not fall when they are ripe, workers cut them down by hand with long knives.

The beans are removed from the pod and placed in wooden boxes, where they are left to ferment for about a week. Fermentation is the stage that creates the taste; without it, chocolate would be bitter and grey. The beans are then spread in the sun to dry, which takes five to ten days and reduces their weight by half.

At the factory, the dried beans are roasted at 120 to 140 degrees. Roasting loosens the shells, which are broken off in a machine called a winnower, leaving small pieces known as nibs. The nibs are ground until the heat turns them into a thick liquid, cocoa mass. At this point sugar, milk powder and extra cocoa butter may be added.

The mixture is then rolled between heavy metal cylinders to make the particles too small for the tongue to feel, and stirred for up to three days in a process called conching, which removes unpleasant flavours. Finally, the chocolate is cooled and warmed again in a careful pattern known as tempering; only tempered chocolate is shiny and breaks with a clean sound.

readings.title: How a plastic bottle becomes a jacket
text: About 480 billion plastic drinks bottles are sold around the world every year, and fewer than half are collected for recycling. Those that are collected can begin a surprising second life as clothing: roughly twenty-five bottles provide enough material for one fleece jacket.

The journey starts at a sorting centre. Bottles arrive mixed with other rubbish, so machines blow air through the moving belt to lift the lightest items, and infrared scanners separate PET bottles from other plastics. Workers then remove anything the machines have missed, such as glass.

Next, the bottles are crushed into bales and washed in hot water to take off the labels and glue. After washing, the plastic is cut into flakes the size of a fingernail. The flakes are dried and heated until they melt, and the liquid plastic is pushed through a metal plate with hundreds of tiny holes, exactly like a shower head. The thin threads that come out are cooled in air, stretched to make them stronger, and wound onto large reels.

The reels go to a textile factory, where the fibre is spun into yarn and knitted into cloth. The cloth is brushed to raise a soft surface, dyed and finally cut and sewn. The whole process uses around 60 per cent less energy than making new polyester from oil, although washing such clothes still releases tiny plastic fibres into the water.

readings.title: Reading #6. Mau Piailug, ocean navigator
text: Mau sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti using traditional methods.

In early 1976, Mau Piailug, a fisherman, led an expedition in which he sailed a traditional Polynesian boat across 2,500 miles of ocean from Hawaii to Tahiti. The Polynesian Voyaging Society had organised the expedition. Its purpose was to find out if seafarers in the distant past could have _found their way_ from _one island to the other_ without navigational instruments, or whether the islands had been populated by accident. At the time, Mau was _the only man alive who knew how to navigate_ just by observing the stars, the wind and the sea.

He had never before sailed to Tahiti, which was a long way to the south. However, he understood how the wind and the sea behave around islands, so he was confident he could find his way. The voyage took him and his crew a month to complete and he did it without a compass or charts.

His grandfather began the task of teaching him how to navigate when he was still a baby. He showed him pools of water on the beach to teach him how the behaviour of the waves and wind changed in different places. Later, Mau used a circle of stones to _memorise_ _the positions of the stars_. Each stone was laid out in the sand to represent a star.

The voyage proved that Hawaii's first inhabitants came in small boats and navigated by reading the sea and the stars. Mau himself became a keen teacher, passing on his traditional secrets to people of other cultures so that his knowledge would not be lost. He explained the positions of the stars to his students, but he allowed them to write things down because he knew they would never be able to remember everything as he had done.

readings.title: Reading #9. Sylvia Earle, underwater hero
readings.qtype: Short answer + True / False / Not Given
text: She has spent her working life studying the world's oceans. Sylvia Earle is an underwater explorer and marine biologist who was born in the USA in 1935. She became interested in the world's oceans from an early age. As a child, she liked to stand on the beach for hours and look at the sea, wondering what it must be like under the surface.

When she was 16, she finally got a chance to make her first dive. It was this dive that inspired her to become an underwater explorer. Since then, she has spent more than 6,500 hours under water, and has led more than seventy expeditions worldwide. She has also made the deepest dive ever, reaching a record-breaking depth of 381 metres.

In 1970, she became famous around the world when she became the captain of the first all-female team to live under water. The team spent two weeks in an underwater 'house'. The research they carried out showed the damage that pollution was causing to marine life, and especially to coral reefs. Her team also studied the problem of over-fishing. Fishing methods meant that people were catching too many fish, Earle warned, and many species were in danger of becoming extinct.

Since then she has written several books and magazine articles in which she suggests ways of reducing the damage that is being done to the world's oceans. One way, she believes, is to rely on fish farms for seafood, and reduce the amount of fishing that is done out at sea. Although she no longer eats seafood herself, she realises the importance it plays in our diets. It would be wrong to tell people they should stop eating fish from the sea, she says. However, they need to reduce the impact they are having on the ocean's supplies.

readings.title: The accident that gave us the microwave
text: In 1945 an American engineer called Percy Spencer was testing a magnetron, a device used in radar equipment during the Second World War. While he stood in front of the machine, he noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. Spencer had left school at twelve and had no university degree, but he had already registered dozens of patents.

Curious, he sent for a bag of popcorn kernels and held them near the magnetron. They popped. The next morning he tried an egg, which exploded in the face of a colleague who leaned over it. Spencer understood that the waves were heating the water inside the food, and that the heat came from the inside out.

The first commercial microwave oven went on sale in 1947. It was nearly two metres tall, weighed 340 kilograms and cost about 5,000 dollars — as much as a house in some parts of the country. Restaurants and ships bought a few, but ordinary families did not.

Everything changed in 1967, when a smaller model appeared for less than 500 dollars. By 1975 microwaves were selling faster than gas cookers in the United States, and today they are found in more than 90 per cent of American homes. Spencer himself received no extra payment for the invention beyond the company's standard bonus of two dollars.

readings.title: The woman who mapped the ocean floor
text: When Marie Tharp finished her geology degree in 1944, American universities were short of male students because of the war, and for the first time women were accepted onto the course. After graduating she moved to New York and found work at Columbia University, where she was given a desk but not a place on the research ships: women were not allowed on board until 1965.

Her colleague Bruce Heezen collected measurements of ocean depth from the Atlantic; Tharp turned thousands of numbers into pictures. Working by hand, she drew the shape of the sea floor, line by line, on long sheets of paper. In 1952 she noticed something nobody expected: a deep valley running along the middle of the underwater mountain chain.

Heezen called her idea "girl talk", because it supported the theory of continental drift, which most scientists then rejected. For almost a year he refused to publish it. Only after the same valley appeared in recordings of underwater earthquakes did he agree that she was right. The discovery became one of the main pieces of evidence for plate tectonics, the idea that the Earth's surface is made of moving plates.

Tharp's name did not appear on the most famous map she helped create, published in 1977, although her drawings were the basis for it. Recognition came late: she received her first major award in 1996, at the age of seventy-six, and the Library of Congress later named her one of the great cartographers of the twentieth century.

readings.title: The first photograph
text: The oldest surviving photograph was taken in 1826 or 1827 by a French inventor, Joseph Nicéphore Niépce, from an upstairs window of his house in Burgundy. The picture shows the roofs of farm buildings and a tree. To make it, Niépce covered a metal plate with a kind of natural tar which hardens in light, and left the plate inside a wooden box with a lens for at least eight hours — some experts believe several days.

Niépce called the process heliography, from the Greek words for "sun" and "writing". He was not trying to make art: his first aim had been to copy printed pictures cheaply. He worked alone for years, spending much of his small income on materials, and received no public attention during his life.

In 1829 he agreed to work with Louis Daguerre, a painter from Paris. Niépce died four years later, and in 1839 Daguerre announced a faster process, the daguerreotype, which needed only a few minutes. The French government bought the invention and gave it to the world; Daguerre became famous, while Niépce's name was almost forgotten for a century.

The original plate was lost for many years and rediscovered in a London storeroom in 1952. It is now kept in Texas in a sealed case filled with a gas that protects it from air. Visitors often say it is difficult to see anything at all: the image is pale, and the light in the photograph comes from both sides, because the sun moved across the sky while the picture was being made.

readings.title: Reading #10. The electric revolution
text: Your next car may be electric. We look at the technologies that will bring the revolution.

The main reasons why electric cars are not more popular at present are their price and their relatively small range. Existing battery systems only allow electric cars to travel a distance of between 100 and 160 km. However, this distance may not be a problem for urban drivers. A recent Sydney study reported that 20 percent of journeys were 30 km or less, and recent data from the US suggests that ?? percent of trips taken there are 48 km or less.

An innovative company called Better Place is aiming to make electric cars an option for all drivers. It wants to see existing vehicles replaced by electric vehicles which, it says, offer a number of benefits. Firstly, they can be powered by renewable energy which produces zero emissions. What is more, electric motors are more efficient and can convert more than 90 percent of power into movement, whereas the efficiency of diesel or petrol engines is less than 20 percent. To achieve its aim, Better Place plans to use technology which is already available.

The plan is simple but revolutionary. It starts with the installation of a home charge point, and through this, the vehicle will be plugged into the electricity grid whenever it is in the garage, typically at night. In the morning, with a fully charged battery, the car is capable of as much as 160 km in urban motoring conditions. In addition to the home charge point, the battery can be topped up by charge points at work and at supermarkets.

The battery is linked to a control centre by smart technology inside the vehicle. Better Place can then ensure that the car is charged with electricity from renewable sources at the cheapest price. For longer trips, a navigation system directs the driver to the nearest switch station, where the depleted battery can be replaced with a charged one by a robot within a couple of minutes.

readings.title: Inside a wind turbine
text: A modern wind turbine looks simple from a distance, but it contains more than eight thousand parts. The structure stands on a concrete base, sometimes twenty metres across, which is buried under the ground. Above this rises the tower, a hollow steel tube with a ladder and, in larger machines, a small lift inside.

At the top of the tower sits a box about the size of a bus. This box is called the nacelle, and it holds the working parts of the machine. Attached to the front of the nacelle is the hub, and three blades are fixed to the hub. Each blade is made of glass fibre and can be longer than eighty metres — longer than the wing of a large aircraft.

Inside the nacelle, the slow turning of the blades, about fifteen times a minute, is passed to a gearbox, which increases the speed to around 1,500 turns a minute. The fast shaft then drives the generator, where movement becomes electricity. Behind the generator, at the back of the nacelle, a small weather station measures wind speed and direction; a motor called the yaw drive turns the whole nacelle so that the blades always face the wind.

The electricity travels down cables inside the tower to a transformer at the base, which raises the voltage so that the power can be carried along the grid. A single large turbine produces enough electricity for about two thousand homes, and modern machines start working in a wind of only three metres a second.

readings.title: How a vacuum flask keeps drinks hot
text: The vacuum flask was invented in 1892 by the Scottish scientist James Dewar, who needed to store extremely cold gases in his laboratory. He never patented it; a German company began selling flasks for tea and coffee eleven years later.

The flask works by stopping the three ways in which heat moves. Its heart is a glass or steel bottle with double walls. The air between the two walls is removed, leaving a vacuum. Because heat cannot travel through empty space by conduction, very little warmth escapes through the sides.

The inner surface of both walls is covered with a thin layer of silver, which acts like a mirror and reflects heat back into the liquid. This stops radiation. At the bottom of the inner bottle there is a small glass point, sealed after the air was taken out; this is the weakest part, so the bottle sits on a soft pad of rubber or foam inside the outer case.

The outer case, usually plastic or metal, protects the fragile bottle and stays cool to touch. At the top, a tight stopper made of plastic or cork closes the neck; this prevents convection, the movement of warm air upwards and out. Many modern flasks add a cup, which screws over the stopper and serves as a lid. Together these parts can keep a drink hot for up to twenty-four hours, though every time the flask is opened it loses several degrees.

readings.title: The parts of a traditional water mill
text: Water mills have ground grain into flour for more than two thousand years, and a few still work in Central Asia and Europe today. The building is usually placed beside a fast stream. Water is taken from the stream further upriver and carried along a narrow channel, called the leat, which runs almost level so that the water arrives above the height of the wheel.

At the end of the leat the water passes through a wooden gate, the sluice, which the miller opens and closes to control the flow. From there it falls onto the wheel. In an overshot mill the water lands in buckets at the top of the wheel and turns it by weight; in an undershot mill the water pushes the bottom of the wheel instead, and less power is produced.

The wheel turns a horizontal beam, the axle, which passes through the wall into the building. Inside, a large wooden gearwheel, the pit wheel, changes the direction of the movement from horizontal to vertical. A vertical shaft then carries the movement upwards to the millstones on the floor above.

There are always two millstones. The lower one, the bed stone, never moves. The upper one, the runner stone, turns just above it, leaving a gap thinner than a sheet of paper. Grain falls into the centre of the runner stone from a wooden box called the hopper, moves outwards between the stones, and leaves the edge as flour, which slides down a wooden chute into sacks on the floor below.

readings.title: Reading #11. The Boeing 787
text: The Boeing 787 'Dreamliner' has been described as the airliner of the future. We look at the technology that makes it different.

Until now, airliner fuselages have been made of aluminium sheets. Large aircraft can have 1,500 of these sheets with between 40,000 and 50,000 metal fasteners. The 787 is the first airliner to be built with a one-piece fuselage made from a special material called 'composite'. Not only does this make the airliner quicker and easier to build, but it also makes it a lot lighter.

The advantage of this weight reduction is that the 787 uses 20 percent less fuel than other airliners of a similar size, which makes it much more environmentally friendly. The reduced weight also means that the Boeing 787 can fly further than many other airliners of a similar size, carrying 210 passengers or more up to 15,200 kilometres before refuelling.

Sometimes an airliner needs to change from one type of engine to another. This is a difficult and time-consuming process. The 787 has a revolutionary engine attachment on the wing which means that the engines can be changed in a much shorter time. The case containing the engine is also different from those on other airliners. It has been designed to cut down the noise from the engine, making it less noisy for passengers in the cabin as well as for people on the ground.

In addition to a quieter cabin, passengers will also benefit from windows which are 65 percent larger than those on other airliners, giving them a much better view of the world passing by below them. The windows also have a unique facility which allows passengers or cabin crew to control the amount of light that enters them. This is thanks to a liquid in the window which reacts to an electric current. When a passenger or cabin crew member presses a button, the current causes a chemical reaction in the window which darkens the liquid.

listenings.title: How a rainwater system works
intro: Uy uchun yomg'ir suvini yig'ish tizimi haqida ma'ruza. Chizmada tizim kesimi. BIR MARTA tinglang.
transcript: SPEAKER: Right, let's look at how a domestic rainwater system actually works. I'll follow the water from the roof down to the tap.
SPEAKER: Rain falls on the roof and runs into the gutter along the edge. Nothing unusual so far. The gutter takes the water to a vertical pipe at the corner of the house — that's the downpipe.
SPEAKER: At the bottom of the downpipe, before anything else, there's a leaf filter. It's a simple mesh basket. Most people forget to clean it, and that's the commonest cause of problems.

SPEAKER: After the filter the water reaches the first flush device. The idea is simple: the first few litres carry dust and bird droppings, so they are sent away and not stored. Once that small chamber is full, the clean water passes on.
SPEAKER: The water then enters the tank, which is usually underground, where the temperature stays low and the water keeps better. A typical family tank holds five thousand litres.
SPEAKER: Inside the tank, notice that the inlet pipe has a smooth curve at the end, called a calmed inlet. It slows the water so that the dirt at the bottom is not stirred up.
SPEAKER: The pump sits either in the tank or beside it; in our diagram it's outside, in the small chamber on the right. It sends water to the house through the supply line.

SPEAKER: Near the top of the tank there's an overflow, which takes extra water away in heavy rain. And finally, at the house end, there's a backflow valve, which makes sure rainwater can never enter the drinking water pipes.

transcript: SPEAKER: Good evening. I'm here to explain how the city bike scheme works, and to answer the question everyone asks: is it actually cheaper than the bus?
SPEAKER: The scheme opened three years ago with 200 bikes at 20 stations. Today there are 1,400 bikes at 130 stations, and we add about ten stations a year.

SPEAKER: Now, prices. A single ride of up to thirty minutes costs one pound fifty. A day pass is five pounds, and an annual membership is sixty. For most people the annual pass pays for itself after about six weeks of daily use.

SPEAKER: The most common complaint is not price, though — it's finding an empty space to leave the bike. In the morning everybody cycles towards the centre, so the central stations fill up. We move bikes back out by van at night, but the vans themselves are unpopular with residents.

SPEAKER: We are testing a solution: users who return a bike to an empty station in the centre get a free ride credit. In the trial, this cut the number of full stations by about a third, which is better than we expected.

SPEAKER: Safety. Helmets are not provided — we know some cities do this, but hygiene rules make it difficult. Instead we spend the money on lights, which are now fitted to every bike and switch on automatically.

SPEAKER: Finally, who uses the bikes? You might expect students, but our data shows that the largest group is people aged between thirty and forty-five, travelling to work. Students actually prefer walking, because the campus is close to the centre.

readings.title: Reading #12. Traffic Jams — No End in Sight
text: A. There are no easy answers to the problems of traffic congestion. Traffic congestion affects people throughout the world. Traffic jams cause smog in dozens of cities across both the developed and developing world. In the U.S., commuters spend an average of a full work week each year sitting in traffic, according to the Texas Transportation Institute. While alternative ways of getting around are available, most people still choose their cars because they are looking for convenience, comfort and privacy.

B. The most promising technique for reducing city traffic is called congestion pricing, whereby cities charge a toll to enter certain parts of town at certain times of day. In theory, if the toll is high enough, some drivers will cancel their trips or go by bus or train. And in practice it seems to work: Singapore, London and Stockholm have reduced traffic and pollution in city centers thanks to congestion pricing.

C. Another way to reduce rush hour traffic is for employers to implement flexitime, which lets employees travel to and from work at off-peak traffic times to avoid the rush hour. Those who have to travel during busy times can do their part by sharing cars. Employers can also allow more staff to telecommute (work from home) so as to keep more cars off the road altogether.

D. Some urban planners still believe that the best way to ease traffic congestion is to build more roads, especially roads that can take drivers around or over crowded city streets. But such techniques do not really keep cars off the road; they only accommodate more of them.

E. Other, more forward-thinking, planners know that more and more drivers and cars are taking to the roads every day, and they are unwilling to encourage more private automobiles when public transport is so much better both for people and the environment. For this reason, the American government has decided to spend some $7 billion on helping to increase capacity on public transport systems and upgrade them with more efficient technologies. But environmentalists complain that such funding is tiny compared with the $50 billion being spent on roads and bridges.

readings.title: Reading #13. Pedestrians only
text: How traffic-free shopping streets developed

A. The concept of traffic-free shopping areas goes back a long time. During the Middle Ages, traffic-free shopping areas known as souks were built in Middle Eastern countries to allow people to shop in comfort and, more importantly, safety. As far back as 2,000 years ago, road traffic was banned from central Rome during the day to allow for the free movement of pedestrians, and was only allowed in at night when shops and markets had closed for the day. In most other cities, however, pedestrians were forced to share the streets with horses, coaches and, later, with cars and other motorised vehicles.

B. The modern, traffic-free shopping street was born in Europe in the 1960s, when both city populations and car ownership increased rapidly. Dirty exhaust fumes from cars and the risks involved in crossing the road were beginning to make shopping an unpleasant and dangerous experience. Many believed the time was right for experimenting with car-free streets, and shopping areas seemed the best place to start.

C. At first, there was resistance from shopkeepers. They believed that such a move would be bad for business. They argued that people would avoid streets if they were unable to get to them in their cars. When the first streets in Europe were closed to traffic, there were even noisy demonstrations, as many shopkeepers predicted they would lose customers.

D. However, research carried out afterwards in several European cities revealed some unexpected statistics. In Munich, Cologne and Hamburg, visitors to shopping areas increased by 50 percent. On Copenhagen's main shopping street, shopkeepers reported sales increases of 25-40 percent. Shopkeepers in Minneapolis, USA, were so impressed when they learnt this that they even offered to pay for the construction and maintenance costs of their own traffic-free streets.

readings.title: Reading #14. Future of money: a currency that helps people make friends
text: A. In one of America's poorest cities, a new use of technology has been attracting attention. The 92,000 people who live in Macon, Georgia, USA know each other a little better than they did, thanks to an online computer game. Since October, the locals - college students and elderly people alike - have been playing Macon Money, a 'social impact game' that uses 'virtual money' to bring people from different economic backgrounds closer together by encouraging them to meet.

B. In the game, winning players receive 'bonds', which they can then exchange for bank notes of Macon Money. These notes can be spent at local shops and businesses. But the game is not as simple as it sounds. Each person receives just half a bond and must find the person with the other half so that they can spend it. People often find their other half by searching for them on the social networking sites Facebook and Twitter. Matching players then meet in person to redeem the bond and get their Macon Money. The bonds range in value from $10 to $100.

C. Pairs might spend their money separately, or do something together like share a meal or give the money to someone who needs it more, says Beverly Blake of the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation, the non-profit group based in Miami, Florida, that funded the game. 'These are meetings and conversations that might not happen naturally at all,' she said. The game's designers are hoping Macon Money will bring members of the community together who wouldn't normally meet each other.

D. Although Macon Money is quite a new innovation, early signs are positive. The first round of the game has seen $65,000-worth of bonds given out and 2,688 participants so far spending $48,000 in Macon Money. Recently, Macon Money's Executive Producer Kati London accepted the 2011 FutureEverything Award for outstanding innovation in art, society and technology in Manchester, UK. It isn't just technology for technology's sake, London said in an interview with FutureEverything after receiving the award, 'It's about putting those tools, that craft, to work in the community.'

E. Whether such a game can bring lasting economic growth remains to be seen, however. An independent research firm will now evaluate how much economic activity the game has caused, with results due later this year.

readings.title: Why city birds sing differently
text: A. Anyone who has walked in a park at dawn knows that birds are noisy in the morning. What fewer people notice is that the same species sounds different in the city and in the countryside. Over the last twenty years biologists in Europe, Asia and North America have recorded thousands of hours of birdsong and found the same pattern almost everywhere.

B. The pattern is simple: city birds sing higher and louder. Traffic produces a deep, low noise, and a low song disappears inside it, like a voice in a busy room. By raising the pitch, a bird lifts its song above the traffic. Great tits in Amsterdam, for example, sing about two hundred hertz higher than great tits in nearby woods.

C. Singing higher solves one problem and creates another. Female birds usually prefer deep songs, which show that a male is large and strong. A male who sings high may be heard, but he may also be judged as weak. Researchers in Germany found that city females took longer to choose a partner, and some pairs produced fewer eggs.

D. Time of day matters as well. In quiet villages, birds begin singing at first light. In cities they often start up to two hours earlier, using the only period when the streets are silent. Street lighting adds to this: under bright lamps, robins sometimes sing through the night, which is exhausting for them.

E. Not every bird can adapt. Species that sing naturally low, such as pigeons, cannot raise their pitch, and they are disappearing from the noisiest districts. Species with flexible voices, like blackbirds and sparrows, are doing well. Over time this changes which birds live around us — noise acts like a filter.

F. Some cities are now responding. Planting trees along busy roads reduces noise by several decibels, and quiet surfaces on roads help too. In one Dutch experiment, after a road was resurfaced, the local great tits lowered their songs again within two years — proof that the change is behaviour, not evolution.

readings.title: The return of the wolf
text: A. A hundred years ago wolves had disappeared from most of Western Europe. Farmers had hunted them, governments had paid rewards for dead animals, and the forests they needed had been cut down. By 1970 only a few hundred survived, mainly in Italy, Spain and Poland.

B. Then the law changed. In 1979 European countries signed an agreement that made killing wolves illegal, and at the same time millions of people were leaving the countryside for the cities. Fields returned to forest, deer and wild boar multiplied, and the wolves followed the food. Today there are more than twenty thousand wolves in Europe, and packs have been photographed within fifty kilometres of Paris and Berlin.

C. Scientists were especially interested in what happened in one American park, where wolves were reintroduced in 1995. Deer had eaten so many young trees that the riverbanks were bare. With wolves present, the deer moved more often and stopped feeding in open valleys; trees grew back, birds returned, and even the rivers changed shape because the banks became stronger.

D. Farmers see the story from another side. A single wolf pack can kill sheep, and in some mountain regions attacks have risen sharply. Governments pay compensation, but the money arrives late and does not cover the fear of losing animals that a family has raised for years. In several countries this has become a political question, not a scientific one.

E. Protection that works is usually old-fashioned. Electric fences help, but the most effective tool is a large guard dog that lives with the flock from birth. In Portugal, farms with such dogs report up to 90 per cent fewer attacks. The problem is cost: a trained dog is expensive, and small farms cannot always afford one.

F. The debate is likely to continue, because both sides are partly right. Wolves make forests healthier, and they are protected by law; but the people who lose animals are real, and telling them that a predator is "good for the ecosystem" solves nothing. Most experts now argue for money and training rather than for new laws.

readings.title: Sleep and the teenage brain
text: A. Parents often complain that teenagers cannot get up in the morning and will not go to bed at night. For a long time this was treated as laziness. Sleep research over the past thirty years suggests something different: the teenage body clock really does move.

B. The clock is controlled by a hormone called melatonin, which tells the body that it is time to sleep. In children, melatonin is released at about nine in the evening. In teenagers it appears one to three hours later, and it also disappears later in the morning. A fifteen-year-old asked to sleep at ten is being asked to sleep while their body is still in "day" mode.

C. The effects of missing sleep are easy to measure. Teenagers who sleep fewer than seven hours make more mistakes in tests of attention, remember less of what they studied, and report more arguments at home. Some studies also link short sleep to weight gain, because tiredness changes the hormones that control hunger.

D. Screens make the situation worse, though perhaps not for the reason most people think. The blue light of a phone does delay melatonin a little, but the bigger problem is what the phone contains: messages that demand an answer and videos designed never to end. A book in bed rarely keeps a teenager awake until two in the morning.

E. Some schools have tried the obvious experiment. In one English town, lessons began at ten instead of nine for two years. Attendance improved, and the number of top grades rose by about twelve per cent. However, parents who started work at eight found the new times difficult, and after the study ended the school returned to the old timetable.

F. Researchers suggest small changes that families can make: the same bedtime every day, including weekends; no screens for an hour before sleep; bright light in the morning to reset the clock. These are less dramatic than changing the school day, but they are free, and every family can try them tonight.

readings.title: Reading #15. Air conditioning
text: The history of an invention that makes life more pleasant
Willis Carrier designed the first air-conditioning unit in 1902, just a year after graduating from Cornell University with a Masters in Engineering.

At a Brooklyn printing plant, _fluctuations in heat and moisture_ were causing the size of the printing paper to keep changing slightly, making it hard to align different colours. Carrier's invention made it possible to control temperature and humidity levels and so align the colours. The invention also allowed industries such as film, processed food, textiles and pharmaceuticals to improve the quality of their products.

In 1914, the first air-conditioning device was installed in a private house. However, its size, similar to that of an early computer, meant it _took up too much space_ to come into widespread use, and later models, such as the Weathermaker, which Carrier brought out in the 1920s, _cost too much_ for most people. Cooling for human comfort, rather than industrial need, really took off when three air conditioners were installed in the J.L. Hudson Department Store in Detroit, Michigan. People crowded into the shop to experience the new invention. The fashion spread from department stores to cinemas, whose income rose steeply as a result of the comfort they provided.

To start with, money-conscious employers regarded air conditioning as a luxury. They considered that if they were paying people to work, they should not be paying for them to be comfortable as well. So in the 1940s and '50s, the industry started _putting out a different message_ about its product: according to their research, installing air conditioning _increased productivity_ amongst employees. They found that typists increased their output by 24% when transferred from a regular office to a cooled one. Another study into office working conditions, which was carried out in the late '50s, showed that the majority of companies cited air conditioning as the single most important contributor to efficiency in offices.

However, air conditioning has its critics. Jed Brown, an environmentalist, complains that air conditioning is _a factor in global warming_. Unfortunately, he adds, because air conditioning leads to higher temperatures, people have to use it even more. However, he admits that it provides _a healthier environment_ for many people in the heat of summer.

readings.title: Reading #16. The ballpoint pen
text: Most of us have at least one, but how did this popular item evolve?

One morning in 1945, a crowd of 5,000 people jammed the entrance of Gimbels Department Store in New York. The day before, Gimbels had placed _a full-page advertisement_ in the New York Times for a wonderful new invention, the ballpoint pen. The advertisement described the pen as _'fantastic' and 'miraculous'_. Although they were expensive, $12.50 each, all 10,000 pens in stock were sold on the first day.

In fact, this 'new' pen was not new at all. In 1888, John Loud, a leather manufacturer, had invented a pen with a reservoir of ink and a rolling ball. However, his pen was _never produced_, and efforts by other people to produce a commercially successful one failed too. The main problem was with the ink. If it was too thin, the ink _leaked out_ of the pen. If it was too thick, it _didn't come out of the pen at all_.

Almost fifty years later, in 1935, a newspaper editor in Hungary thought he spent too much time filling his pens with ink. He decided to invent a better kind of pen. With the help of his brother, who was a chemist, he produced a ballpoint pen that _didn't leak when the pen wasn't being used_. The editor was called Ladislas Biro, and it was his name that people would associate more than any other with the ballpoint pen.

By chance, Biro met Augustine Justo, the Argentinian president. Justo was so impressed with Biro's invention that he invited him to set up a factory in Argentina. In 1943, the first Biro pens were produced.

Unfortunately, they were not popular, since the pen _needed to be held in a vertical position_ for the ink to come out. Biro redesigned the pen with a better ball, and in 1944 the new product was on sale throughout Argentina.

It was a North American, Milton Reynolds, who introduced the ballpoint pen to the USA. Copying Biro's design, he produced the version that sold so well at Gimbels. Another American, Patrick Frawley, _improved the design_ and in 1950 began producing a pen he called the Papermate. It was _an immediate success_, and within a few years, Papermates were selling in their millions _around the world_.

readings.title: Why we believe things that are not true
text: Most people think of memory as a recording: something happens, the brain stores it, and later we play it back. Psychologists have shown that this picture is wrong. Memory is closer to a story that we rebuild each time we tell it, and small changes appear at every telling.

In a famous series of experiments in the 1970s, Elizabeth Loftus showed volunteers a short film of a car accident and then asked them questions about it. One group was asked how fast the cars were going when they "hit" each other; another group heard the word "smashed". A week later, those who had heard "smashed" were more than twice as likely to say they had seen broken glass, although there was no broken glass in the film at all.

This does not mean that people were lying. The brain fills gaps automatically, using what seems reasonable. If a word suggests a violent crash, broken glass becomes part of the reasonable picture, and the memory is updated without our permission. Later, the false detail feels exactly like a true one; confidence is no guide to accuracy.

The effect matters outside the laboratory. Courts have relied for centuries on witnesses who say they are certain, and studies of prisoners later cleared by DNA evidence found that mistaken identification played a part in about seventy per cent of the cases. Police forces in several countries now show photographs one at a time rather than together, because comparing faces encourages the brain to choose the "best match" rather than the right one.

None of this makes memory useless. For the general shape of events — who was there, what happened first — it is usually reliable. The danger lies in small, confident details, and the solution is not to trust less but to check more: write things down, keep records, and treat a vivid memory as a good story rather than as evidence.

readings.title: The four-day week experiment
text: Between June and December 2022, sixty-one British companies took part in the largest trial of a four-day working week ever organised. About 2,900 employees worked one day less each week for the same pay, on the condition that they maintained their previous level of output.

The companies were of many kinds: software firms, a fish-and-chip shop, a charity, a bank, a small brewery. Researchers from three universities collected data before, during and after the trial. When it ended, fifty-six of the sixty-one companies decided to continue, and eighteen made the change permanent immediately.

The results that attracted most attention were about health. Employees reported that anxiety and tiredness fell, and the number of sick days dropped by about two thirds. The number of staff leaving their jobs fell by more than half compared with the same period a year earlier — a figure that matters to employers, because replacing a trained worker is expensive.

Output did not fall. Company revenue during the trial was slightly higher than in the same months of the previous year, although researchers warned that six months is too short a period to be certain, and that companies willing to join such a trial may be unusual. Some firms achieved the change by shortening meetings; one limited meetings to fifteen minutes unless a longer time was agreed in advance.

Not everything worked smoothly. Businesses that deal with the public, such as shops and clinics, found it harder, because somebody must be present every day; they used staggered days off rather than closing. A few employees said that four longer days left them more tired, and preferred the old pattern. The researchers' conclusion was careful: the model suits many offices, but it is not a rule that fits every workplace.

readings.title: The language that has no numbers
text: In the Amazon rainforest lives a small community, the Pirahã, whose language has fascinated linguists for fifty years. Its most famous feature is what it lacks: there are no words for exact numbers. Speakers use three quantity words, usually translated as "few", "some" and "many", and the same word can mean one or two depending on the situation.

Daniel Everett, who lived with the group for years, tested this with a simple task. He put out a line of batteries and asked speakers to copy it. With two or three objects they were accurate; with eight or ten, performance fell sharply, even though they clearly understood the task and wanted to succeed. Later researchers repeated the experiment with the same result.

For some scientists this supports a strong claim: that the words a language gives us shape what we can think. Others reject that conclusion. They point out that the Pirahã can learn to count if they wish, and that a few adults did so during a course they themselves requested, although they lost the skill when the classes stopped. Not having a tool, these researchers argue, is different from being unable to use one.

What is clear is that exact counting is not automatic in humans. Archaeologists find counting marks on bones from at least 20,000 years ago, but writing systems for numbers are much younger, and several languages around the world stop at "three" before moving to "many". Children everywhere learn number words slowly, one at a time, and often take a year to move from "two" to "three" — which suggests that counting is invented and taught, not born with us.

The Pirahã themselves are not troubled by the debate. When Everett asked why they did not want to count, one man answered that they had everything they needed and did not wish to store things — a reply that says as much about economics as about language.

readings.title: Reading #17. Rubik's Cube - How the puzzle achieved success
text: Erno Rubik first studied sculpture and then later architecture in Budapest, where he went on to become a teacher of interior design. It was while he was working as a teacher that he began the preliminary work on an invention that he called the 'Magic Cube'.

Rubik was inspired by geometric puzzles such as the Chinese tangram, a puzzle consisting of various triangles, a square and a parallelogram which can be combined to create different shapes and figures. However, unlike the tangram, which is two-dimensional, Rubik was more interested in investigating how three-dimensional forms, such as the cube, could be moved and combined to produce other forms.

His design consisted of a cube made up of layers of individual smaller cubes, and each smaller cube could be turned in any direction except diagonally. To ensure that the cubes could move independently, without falling apart, Rubik first attempted to join them together using elastic bands. However, this proved to be impossible, so Rubik then solved the problem by assembling them using a rounded interior. This permitted them to move smoothly and easily. He experimented with different ways of marking the smaller cubes, but ended up with the simple solution of giving a different colour to each side. The object was to twist the layers of small cubes so that each side of the large cube was an identical colour.

Rubik took out a patent for the Cube in 1977 and started manufacturing it in the same year. The Cube came to the attention of a Hungarian businessman, Tibor Laczi, who then demonstrated it at the Nuremberg Toy Fair. When British toy expert Tom Kremer saw it, he thought it was amazing and he persuaded a manufacturer, Ideal Toys, to produce 1 million of them in 1979. Ideal Toys renamed the Cube after the toy's inventor, and in 1980, Rubik's Cube was shown at toy fairs all over the world. It won that year's prize in Germany for Best Puzzle. Rubik's Cube is believed to be the world's best-selling puzzle; since its invention, more than 300 million Cubes have been sold worldwide.

readings.title: Reading #18. Marcel Bich
text: The man who turned a luxury item into an everyday object

Marcel Bich, a French manufacturer of traditional ink pens, was the man who turned the ballpoint pen into an item that today almost anyone can afford. Bich was appalled at the poor quality of the ballpoint pens that were available, and was also shocked at their high cost. However, he recognised that the ballpoint was a firmly established invention, and he decided to design a cheap pen that worked well and would be commercially successful.

Bich went to the Biro brothers and asked them if he could use the design of their original invention in one of his own pens. In return, he offered to pay them every time he sold a pen. Then, for two years, Bich studied the detailed construction of every ballpoint pen that was being sold, often working with a microscope.

By 1950, he was ready to introduce his new wonder: a plastic pen with a clear barrel that wrote smoothly, did not leak and only cost a few cents. He called it the 'Bic Cristal'. The ballpoint pen had finally become a practical writing instrument. The public liked it immediately, and today it is as common as the pencil. In Britain, they are still called Biros, and many Bic models also say 'Biro' on the side of the pen, to remind people of their original inventors.

Bich became extremely wealthy thanks to his invention, which had worldwide appeal. Over the next 60 years his company, Societe Bic, opened factories all over the world and expanded its range of inexpensive products. Today, Bic is as famous for its lighters and razors as it is for its pens, and you can even buy a Bic mobile phone.

readings.title: The sticky note that nobody wanted
text: In 1968 Spencer Silver, a chemist at the American company 3M, was trying to develop a very strong glue for aircraft. Instead, he made the opposite: an adhesive so weak that it could be pulled off a surface without leaving a mark. Silver believed the glue must be useful for something, and for five years he gave talks about it inside the company. Nobody could think of a practical use.

The solution came from a colleague, Art Fry, who sang in a church choir. Every Sunday the paper bookmarks in his hymn book fell out. Fry remembered Silver's glue and put a little on the edge of a bookmark. It stayed in place, and it could be removed without damaging the pages.

The company was not impressed. Managers thought people would never pay for small pieces of paper when free scrap paper was everywhere. A first test in four cities in 1977 failed, because shoppers did not understand what the product was for. The next year, 3M tried a different approach: in the city of Boise, Idaho, it gave free samples to offices. Ninety percent of the people who tried them said they would buy them.

Post-it Notes went on sale across the United States in 1980 and in Europe a year later. Today they are sold in more than 150 countries, and the original yellow colour was chosen by accident — it was the only scrap paper available in the laboratory next door.

readings.title: The invention of the bar code
text: In 1948 a supermarket owner in Philadelphia visited a local university and asked whether there was a way to record product information automatically at the checkout. A graduate student, Bernard Silver, overheard the conversation and told his friend Joseph Woodland, a teacher of mechanical engineering.

Woodland left his job and moved to his grandfather's flat in Florida to think about the problem. Sitting on the beach one day, he pushed his fingers into the sand and pulled them towards him, making four lines. He realised that lines of different widths could be used like the dots and dashes of Morse code. His first design, however, was circular, like a target, so that it could be read from any direction.

The two men received a patent in 1952, but the technology to read the codes did not yet exist. The scanners of the time were enormous and expensive, and the idea was ignored for twenty years. Only when cheap lasers and computers appeared in the early 1970s did supermarkets become interested. A committee chose a rectangular design, which was easier to print than a circle.

The first product ever scanned was a packet of chewing gum, in Ohio, on 26 June 1974. The packet is now kept in a museum in Washington. Today about six billion bar codes are scanned every day, and Woodland, who earned almost nothing from the patent, was given a national medal for technology in 1992.

readings.title: The man who made the world wear jeans
text: In 1853 a young German immigrant, Levi Strauss, opened a shop in San Francisco selling cloth, blankets and clothing to the gold miners of California. The miners' trousers wore out quickly, and customers often complained that the pockets tore when they filled them with tools and pieces of gold.

One of Strauss's regular customers was a tailor in Nevada called Jacob Davis. A woman had asked Davis to make strong trousers for her husband, and Davis had the idea of putting small metal pins, called rivets, at the corners of the pockets, the points which usually tore first. The trousers were so successful that other workers soon wanted a pair.

Davis did not have the money to register a patent, which cost 68 dollars, so he wrote to Strauss and offered to share it if Strauss paid. In 1873 the two men received the patent together, and Strauss brought Davis to San Francisco to manage production.

The first "waist overalls", as they were called, were made from a heavy blue cotton cloth called denim. For almost eighty years jeans were working clothes for farmers, miners and factory workers. Only in the 1950s, when film stars wore them on screen, did young people begin to see jeans as fashionable. Today more than two billion pairs are sold every year.

readings.title: Reading #20. The honey badger
text: It looks harmless and vulnerable. But the honey badger is afraid of nothing... and will attack and eat almost anything

The honey badger (Mellivora capensis) is an African and south-Asian mammal that has a reputation for being one of the world's most fearless animals, _despite its small size_. And in spite of its gentle-sounding name, it is also one of its most _aggressive_. Honey badgers have been known to attack lions, buffalo, and snakes three times their size. Even _humans_ are not safe from a honey badger _if it thinks the human will attack or harm it_. They are also extremely tough creatures, and can recover quickly from injuries that would kill most other animals.

At first glance, honey badgers look like the common European badger. They are usually between 75cm and 1 metre long, although males are about twice the size of females. They are instantly _recognisable_ by grey and white stripes that extend from the top of the head to the tail. Closer inspection, which is probably not a wise thing to do, reveals pointed teeth, and sharp front claws which can be four centimetres in length.

Honey badgers are _meat-eating_ animals with an extremely _varied_ diet. They _mainly eat_ a range of _small creatures_ like beetles, lizards and birds, but will also catch larger reptiles like snakes and small crocodiles. Some mammals, such as foxes, antelope and wild cats also form part of their diet.

The badgers _locate their prey_ mainly using their excellent sense of _smell_, and catch most of their prey through digging. During a 24-hour period, they may dig as many as fifty holes, and travel more than 40 kilometres. They are also good climbers, and can easily climb very tall trees to steal eggs from birds' nests, or catch other tree-dwelling creatures.

As their name suggests, honey badgers have always been associated with honey, although they do not actually eat it. It is the highly nutritious bee eggs (called 'brood') that they prefer, and they will do anything to find it. They usually cause a lot of damage to the hive in the process, and for this reason, humans are one of their main predators. Bee-keepers will often set _special traps_ for honey badgers, to protect their hives.

One of the most fascinating aspects of the honey badger is its _working relationship_ with a bird called the greater honeyguide (Indicator indicator). This bird deliberately guides the badger to beehives, then waits while the badger breaks into the hive and extracts the brood. The two creatures, bird and mammal, then share the brood between them.

readings.title: The octopus: a clever escape artist
text: In April 2016, staff at the National Aquarium of New Zealand arrived at work to find that one of their animals had disappeared. Inky, a male octopus, had pushed his way through a small gap at the top of his tank, travelled across the floor, and escaped down a drainpipe that led directly to the sea. The only evidence of his journey was a wet trail on the floor.

Stories like this are not unusual, because octopuses are among the most intelligent animals without a backbone. An octopus has around 500 million nerve cells, a number similar to that of a dog, but about two thirds of them are found not in its head but in its eight arms. As a result, each arm can taste, touch and even make simple decisions on its own.

The octopus is also a master of disguise. Special cells in its skin allow it to change colour in less than a second, so that it can hide against rocks or sand. Some species can even change the texture of their skin to look like coral. When this does not work, an octopus can release a cloud of dark ink, which confuses an attacker and gives the octopus time to swim away.
Its body is unusual in other ways too. An octopus has three hearts and blue blood, and because it has no bones, it can squeeze through any hole larger than its beak — the only hard part of its body.
Sadly, this remarkable life is short. Most species live for only one or two years, and a female usually dies soon after her eggs hatch, having stopped eating while she guarded them.

readings.title: How camels survive the desert
text: Many people believe that a camel stores water in its hump. In fact, the hump is made mostly of fat. When food is scarce, the camel's body breaks down this fat for energy, and the hump becomes smaller and may even fall to one side. A well-fed camel has a firm, upright hump.

The real secret of the camel's survival lies in how it uses water. A camel can lose up to a quarter of its body weight through water loss and still survive, while most mammals would die after losing half that amount. When it finally finds water, it can drink more than 100 litres in about ten minutes.
Its blood is also unusual. The red blood cells of a camel are oval rather than round, which allows them to keep flowing even when the blood becomes thick because the animal is short of water.

Camels also save water by not sweating very much. Their body temperature can rise by around six degrees during a hot day before they begin to sweat, and the heat stored in their body is released during the cold desert night.

Finally, a camel is well protected from sand. It has two rows of long eyelashes, and it can close its nostrils completely during a sandstorm. Wide, soft feet stop it from sinking into the sand, which is why camels are sometimes called "ships of the desert". For thousands of years, these features have made them the most reliable form of transport for people living in dry regions.
