readings.title: The return of the wolves
text: By the 1920s, grey wolves had disappeared from Yellowstone, the oldest national park in the United States. Farmers and hunters had killed them to protect their animals, and for the next seventy years the park had no large predator at the top of its food chain.

Without wolves, the number of elk, a large kind of deer, grew quickly. The elk spent long periods feeding beside rivers, where they ate young willow and aspen trees before they could grow. Scientists noticed that very few new trees were appearing along the riverbanks.

In 1995 and 1996, thirty-one wolves were caught in Canada and released in the park. Their numbers rose steadily, and within ten years there were more than a hundred. The wolves hunted elk, but they also changed the way elk behaved: the deer began to avoid open river valleys where they could easily be attacked.
In several areas, willow trees started to recover. Beavers, which use willow for food and for building dams, returned in larger numbers, and their dams created pools where fish and birds could live.

However, researchers warn against telling this as a simple story. Hard winters, human hunting and the return of bears also reduced elk numbers, and in some places the trees have not come back at all. Most scientists now agree that the wolves played an important part in the changes, but not the only one — and that nature rarely has a single cause.

readings.title: Reading #21. Humpback whale breaks migration record
text: A whale surprises researchers with her journey.
A lone humpback whale travelled more than 9,800 kilometres from breeding areas in Brazil to those in Madagascar, setting a record for the longest mammal migration ever documented.

Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) are known to have some of the longest migration distances of all mammals, and this huge journey is about 400 kilometres _farther_ than the previous humpback record. The finding was made by Peter Stevick, a biologist at the College of the Atlantic in Bar Harbor, Maine.

The whale's journey was unusual not only for its _length_, but also because it travelled across almost 90 degrees of longitude _from west to east_. Typically, humpbacks move in a north-south direction between _cold feeding areas_ and _warm breeding grounds_ - and the longest journeys which have been recorded until now have been between breeding and feeding sites.

The whale, a female, was first spotted off the coast of Brazil, where researchers _photographed_ its tail fluke and _took skin samples_ for chromosome testing to determine the animal's sex. Two years later, a tourist on a whale-watching boat snapped a photo of the humpback near Madagascar.

To match the two sightings, Stevick's team used an extensive international catalogue of photographs of the undersides of tail flukes, which have distinctive markings. Researchers routinely _compare the markings_ in each new photograph to those in the archive.

The scientists then estimated the animal's shortest possible route: an arc _skirting the southern tip of South Africa_ and heading north-east towards Madagascar. The minimum distance is 9,800 kilometres, says Stevick, but this is likely to be an underestimate, because the whale probably took a detour to feed on krill in the Southern Ocean _near Antarctica_ before reaching its destination.

Most humpback-whale researchers focus their efforts on the Northern Hemisphere because the Southern Ocean near the Antarctic is _a hostile environment_ and it is _hard to get to_, explains Rochelle Constantine, who studies the ecology of humpback whales at the University of Auckland in New Zealand. But, for whales, oceans in the Southern Hemisphere are wider and easier to travel across, says Constantine. Scientists will probably observe more long-distance migrations in the Southern Hemisphere as _satellite tracking_ becomes increasingly common, she adds.

Daniel Palacios, an oceanographer at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, says that the record-breaking journey could indicate that migration patterns are shifting as populations begin to recover from near-extinction and the population increases. But the reasons why the whale did not follow the usual migration routes remain a mystery. She could have been _exploring new habitats_, or simply have _lost her way_. 'We generally think of humpback whales as very well studied, but then they surprise us with things like this,' Palacios says. 'Undoubtedly there are a lot of things we still don't know about whale migration.'

readings.title: Reading #22. On the trail of the honey badger
readings.qtype: Pick from a list (1–5) — qo'shimcha mashq
text: Researchers learn more about this fearless African predator

On a recent field trip to the Kalahari Desert, a team of researchers learnt a lot more about honey badgers. They were rewarded with a detailed insight into how these fascinating creatures live and hunt.

The team employed a local wildlife expert, Kitso Khama, to help them locate and follow the badgers across the desert. Their main aim was _to study the badgers' movements and behaviour_ as discreetly as possible, without frightening them away or causing them to change their natural behaviour. They also planned _to trap a few and study them close up before releasing them_. In view of the animal's reputation, this was something that even Khama was reluctant to do.

'The problem with honey badgers is they are naturally _curious_ animals, especially when they see _something new_,' he says. 'That, combined with their _unpredictable_ nature, can be a dangerous mixture. If they sense you have food, for example, they won't be shy about coming right up to you for something to eat. They're actually quite sociable creatures around humans, but as soon as they feel they might be in danger, they can become extremely vicious. Fortunately this is _rare_, but it does happen.'

The research confirmed many things that were already known. As expected, honey badgers ate any creatures they could catch and kill. Even poisonous snakes, feared and avoided by most other animals, were not safe from them. The researchers were surprised, however, by the animal's fondness for local _melons_, probably because of their _high water content_. Previously researchers thought that the animal got all of its liquid requirements from its prey. The team also learnt that, contrary to previous research findings, the badgers occasionally formed _loose family groups_. They were also able to confirm certain results from previous research, including the fact that female badgers never socialised _with each other_.

Following some of the male badgers was a challenge, since they can cover large distances in a short space of time. Some hunting territories cover _more than 500 square kilometres_. Although they seem happy to share these territories with other males, there are _occasional fights_ over an important food source, and male badgers can be as aggressive towards each other as they are towards other species.

As the badgers became accustomed to the presence of people, it gave the team the chance to get up close to them _without being the subject of the animals' curiosity_ - or their sudden aggression. The badgers' eating patterns, which had been disrupted, returned to normal. It also allowed the team to observe more closely some of the other creatures that form working associations with the honey badger, as these seemed to _adopt the badgers' relaxed attitude_ when near humans.

readings.title: Why birds fly in a V
text: Anyone who has watched geese crossing an autumn sky has noticed their V-shaped formation. For a long time, scientists suspected that the shape helped birds save energy, but it was very difficult to prove, because it is hard to measure what a bird is doing in the air.

In 2014, a team from the Royal Veterinary College in London found a solution. They attached tiny data recorders to a group of northern bald ibises, rare birds that had been trained to follow a light aircraft on their migration. The recorders measured the position of each bird and every beat of its wings.

The results were surprising. Each bird flew in exactly the place where the air pushed up by the wings of the bird in front could help lift it. The birds also timed their wing beats to match the bird ahead, so that they always met rising air rather than falling air. Earlier research on pelicans had shown that birds flying in formation have lower heart rates than those flying alone.

Flying at the front is the hardest job, and no single bird does it all the time. The ibises regularly changed places, and each bird spent roughly as long leading as it did following — a kind of fair sharing that researchers had not expected.

Energy is not the only reason for the shape. A V also allows every bird to see the others clearly, which helps the group stay together and avoid collisions. Young birds on their first migration can follow experienced adults who know the route.

readings.title: The dance of the honeybee
text: When a honeybee discovers a good source of food, it returns to the hive and performs a dance. For centuries, beekeepers noticed this strange movement, but it was the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch who first explained what it meant. His work on bee communication won him a share of the Nobel Prize in 1973.

Von Frisch found that bees use two main dances. If the flowers are close to the hive, a bee performs a "round dance", running in small circles. This tells the other bees that food is nearby, but not the exact direction. For food further away, the bee performs a "waggle dance": it runs forward in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the movement.

The waggle dance contains surprisingly precise information. The angle of the straight run compared with a vertical line on the honeycomb shows the direction of the food compared with the position of the sun. The length of time the bee spends waggling shows how far away the food is: the longer the waggle, the greater the distance.

The dancer also shares other clues. Other bees touch it with their antennae and learn the smell of the flowers it has visited, and they may taste samples of nectar it brings back. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, bees also adjust the angle of their dance as time passes.
Not every scientist accepted von Frisch's ideas at first. Some believed that bees found food only by smell, and it took several decades of experiments before the dance language was widely accepted.

readings.title: How animals sleep
text: All animals with a brain seem to need some form of sleep, but the way they sleep varies enormously. Some of the most unusual examples come from animals that cannot simply lie down and close their eyes.

Dolphins, for example, must come to the surface to breathe, so they can never become fully unconscious. Instead, they rest one half of the brain at a time, while the other half stays awake to control breathing and watch for danger. During this kind of sleep, a dolphin often keeps one eye open.

Frigatebirds, which fly over the ocean for weeks without landing, use a similar method. In 2016, scientists fitted small devices to their heads and discovered that the birds slept in the air, sometimes with one half of the brain and sometimes with both. However, they slept for only about forty minutes a day in flight, compared with more than twelve hours on land.
At the other extreme, some bats sleep for up to twenty hours a day. Scientists believe this saves energy and keeps them away from danger at times when the insects they eat are not active.

Large grazing animals sleep much less. Giraffes and elephants in the wild may sleep for only two to four hours, often in short periods, because they need to spend a long time eating and must stay alert to predators. Why sleep is so necessary is still not fully understood, but its loss causes serious problems in every animal that has been studied.
